details:
Open the tool: https://spaceapps2026.researchedtechnologies.org/

The demo video: https://spaceapps2026.researchedtechnologies.org/demo/lunimartian-atlas-demo.mp4

The code and the method: https://github.com/1004genre/nasalunarbase-26

WHAT IT DOES:
LuniMartian Atlas finds the best places on Earth for a test of Moon or Mars work. A team can then test rovers, cameras, instruments and crews on Earth before the mission.
A scientist uses it in three steps:


1. Select a site: one of the 16 candidate lunar regions that NASA studied, or one of 57 Mars sites.
2. Type or paste the experiment brief. AI models on our own server change the words into conditions.
3. Read the ranked places. Each place has a match percent, its best dates and its evidence.
It is not necessary to fill a long form.

THE EXPERIMENT BOARD AND THE AI:

- The board has 10 categories and approximately 100 conditions. Each category is closed at the start, thus the page stays simple.
- Each condition has an importance from 0 to 10. A 10 means that the condition is necessary.
- The AI models only set conditions. All places and all figures come from the data.
- The page shows the words that it used and the words that it did not use.
- One test: "A quiet place with frozen ground for a seismometer. It must be near an airport. A nice hotel if possible."
- The page set three conditions: human influence, permafrost zone, and distance to an airfield as necessary. It showed the hotel phrase as not used.

WHAT A TEAM LEARNS ABOUT EACH PLACE:
A test site must be practical, and not only similar. For each area, the Atlas shows:
- Access: the distance to an airfield and to a road, and if help is within reach.
- People: the human influence, for example vibration from vehicles and aircraft, radio noise, artificial light and tracks in camera views.
- Power: the yield of a solar panel under the real sky with its cloud, the months without Sun, and the wind at 50 m.
- Climate: cloud, clear-sky days, air temperature, snow-free ground and wind.
- Ground: slope, roughness, rock type and permafrost.
- Hazards: small tremors and volcanoes.
- Land status: who owns or governs the ground, and whom to ask for a permit, as a rough estimate.
- Light: the hours with the Sun as low as at the lunar region, and the best dates.
Each figure has a mark: measured, coarse map, model or rough estimate. An unknown value stays "unknown".

HOW IT WORKS:
1. Open data gives 39 factors: airfields, roads, settlements, land status, cloud, wind, earthquakes, volcanoes and more.
2. For the light, our code counts the hours with the Sun as low as at the lunar region. It uses only the spells of 2 hours or more.
3. Snow maps and a terrain model of Earth remove the hours with snow and the hours that hills hide.
4. Two AI models on our own server change the brief into conditions. They can select only from the list of conditions.
5. An importance of 10 removes each area that fails the condition. Each other condition gives a score from 0 to 1. The match percent is the mean of the known scores, weighted by importance.

HOW WE CHECKED IT
- NASA JPL Horizons: with a flat horizon, we compared 144 results of our Sun code with Horizons. The median difference was 0.009 hours in a ten-day period, and the largest was 0.63 hours.
- Hills: if the code ignores the hills, only 1 of the 10 best areas for Connecting Ridge stays in the top 10. For Malapert Massif, 7 of the 10 stay.
- Known analog sites: for Malapert Massif, the area with the best light score keeps 234 hours of low Sun a year. Haughton crater keeps 102 hours, and the McMurdo Dry Valleys keep less than 20 hours.
- New places: 9 of the 10 best areas for Malapert Massif are more than 300 km from each of our 85 known analog sites.
- Lower latitudes: 11 well-known places get low Sun, but no place has a spell of 2 hours.
- Mars: against approximately 2,000 control squares, known analog squares give an AUC of 0.821 for Jezero crater (0.5 is chance). But bare ground alone gives 0.803. On bare squares only, the result is weak (0.612) to no better than chance (0.464).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
On one page, field-test teams get:
- the place and its best dates;
- the nearest airfield and road;
- the human influence and the hazards;
- the land status and whom to ask for a permit, as a rough estimate;
- the power from the Sun, the wind and the heat of the ground.
A team can compare places before it pays for a field trip.
Intended impact: teams find and correct problems on Earth, before the mission.

TOOLS
- Data: Python, NumPy and Rasterio, with 62 credited sources.
- The page: JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with globe.gl. It has no login and no tracker.
- Hardware: our own server, with nginx, Docker and Ollama (Qwen2.5 7B and nomic-embed-text).
- AI for the work: Claude (Anthropic, through Claude Code) researched, proposed directions, and wrote the pipeline code and first drafts. OpenAI Codex wrote most of the page code.
- People: the team lead selected the challenge, the direction, the factors, the sites and the experiment board.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE
- A scientist describes an experiment in words, and the page sets the conditions.
- The AI models never name a place or give a figure.
- The Atlas ranks a place on practical conditions also: access, people, power and permits.
- It shows, hour by hour, where Earth has the low Sun of a lunar region.
- The text of the page follows the writing rules of ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English.

FACTORS THAT WE CONSIDERED
- Ease of use: a short first page, a phone layout and keyboard use.
- Honest evidence marks and limits.
- Access, permits and power, because a team must work at the place.

Next Steps:

  1. Interviewing scientists about their needs & their user experience with our tool.
  2. Integrating with bigger models that can ingest real experimental documents.
  3. We want to add a functionality where it can compare a list of locations with matching scores and give us pros and cons of each location.
  4. Deterministic guide on factors for both scientists and our model.
